title: Public land in Mato Grosso, Pará and Maranhão sold to colonisers and companies
government: State of Mato Grosso; federal INCRA and Sudam (Maranhão: state company COMARCO)
what: Millions of hectares of public land in Mato Grosso passed through state land bodies to colonisers and companies. In Maranhão, COMARCO (Dec 1971) took in 2.1 million ha of public land at once. No hectare series for Pará.
who_got: Private colonisers SINOP, INDECO and CONTRIGUAÇU, and nominee buyers ('laranjas'). Who financed the buyers: Sudam tax incentives or their own resale. 1970s per-hectare prices were not found.
terms: 1950-64: colonisers paid Cr$7-10 per ha and resold at Cr$100-300 per ha, with average holdings of 200,000 ha.
mechanism: Titles above the 3,000 ha constitutional limit were arranged through powers of attorney to nominee buyers. Decreto-Lei 1.164/1971 put about 60% of Mato Grosso under federal control until 1978. State companies CODEMAT and INTERMAT, and INCRA, then collected and sold land.
who_paid: The public domain, and the Indigenous and posseiro occupants. Settlers paid high resale prices.
after: The state land department (DTC) was closed in 1966 after repeated fraud. Programmes named 'Terra Pública' or direct INCRA sales to companies were not found in any opened source.
counter_view: The sales were also how the state settled the north. The authors' main complaint is the lack of control, fraud and speculation, not the settlement itself (Moreno 1999 via Lilian da Rosa 2017).

figures.value: bought at Cr$7-10 per ha, resold at Cr$100-300 per ha; average 200,000 ha each
figures.note: Secondary summary of Moreno 1999. Holdings were above the 100,000 ha limit that needed Senate approval.

figures.value: more than 6 million ha collected; more than 5 million ha sold in the north
figures.note: Aripuanã, Juruena, Alta Floresta, Juína and others.

figures.value: INTERMAT about 6.4 million ha; INCRA more than 7 million ha collected and about 3.6 million ha titled along federal highways

figures.label: COMARCO (Maranhão) public land taken in, Dec 1971

summary: State land bodies in Mato Grosso collected and sold millions of hectares of public land to colonisers and companies. Titles above the legal limit were arranged through nominee buyers. Hectare data for Pará are missing.

title: Cubatão industrial pole (São Paulo)
what: A state-led industrial pole (Petrobras refinery 1955, Cosipa steel, petrochemical plants) where pollution costs fell on residents. Weak fit for 'public assets to private': it is a case of private firms pushing environmental cost onto others under a regime with no environmental law and no press freedom. Keep as a short note.
who_got: Not applicable.
terms: Not applicable.
mechanism: No environmental regulation (per the note).
who_paid: Residents. 37 stillbirths of 1,800 births (Oct 1981-Apr 1982) came from a mayor's opinion piece. At Vila Socó a gasoline leak of 700,000 litres from a Petrobras pipeline caused the fire of 24 Feb 1984.
after: Vila Socó fire 24 Feb 1984; 'Vale da Morte' label in the early 1980s.
counter_view: Petrobras's then-president Sigeaki Ueki says the company never admitted 500 dead and 'there is no proof' (Agência Brasil).

figures.label: Vila Socó fire deaths
figures.value: 93 (official count); believed up to 508 (MP/commission); residents say 500 or more
figures.note: The earlier note's 'one source says 11' is wrong: 11 is the P-36 platform toll (2001), so it was dropped.

figures.label: Stillbirths in Cubatão
figures.note: Weak source. A study by R. Monteleone Neto found 10,218 live births and 160 stillbirths for Jun 1982 - Dec 1985, a different period.

summary: Cubatão was a state-led industrial pole whose pollution fell on residents. The Vila Socó fire of 1984 killed 93 officially, and perhaps far more. It is a weak fit for the study and kept as a short note.

title: Hanna / MBR iron ore and the 1967 Mining Code (Minas Gerais)
government: Quadros and Goulart (cancellation); Castelo Branco and Costa e Silva (new rules and MBR)
what: Iron, manganese and bauxite deposit rights in the Quadrilátero Ferrífero held by Hanna's Novalimense (Águas Claras, Capão do Xavier, Pico do Itabirito and others). A 1962 order by minister Gabriel Passos voided the registrations. Tonnage and hectares are not given in the sources.
who_got: Caemi (Augusto Antunes) and M. A. Hanna, through MBR, formed in 1965. Who financed them: not found.
terms: No price or compensation figure found. The terms of the 1967 settlement and who got which deposit are unverified.
mechanism: On 23 Dec 1964 Castelo Branco signed a decree letting private and foreign capital into subsoil exploration (oil, coal, nuclear minerals and hydraulic reserves excluded). Decreto-Lei 227/1967 (Mining Code, 28 Feb 1967) followed; its full text on who may hold concessions was not confirmed. MBR was the merger solution. No source shows a formal annulment of the 1962 order, so 'restored by the dictatorship' is unconfirmed.
who_paid: The national mineral patrimony. Not quantified.
after: Hanna and the Antunes group sued in Aug 1962; the Supreme Court sent the question back to the government, and it was settled under Costa e Silva in 1967. Vale bought out Caemi in 2001-2006 and took 100% of MBR in 2007.
counter_view: The companies argued the 1938 registrations were lawful and vested, and that the 1962 order was a ministerial despacho, not a decree. US ambassador Lincoln Gordon protested, and Novalimense president Lucas Lopes called the order illegal (niepmarx). ICOMI director Glycon de Paiva argued that more state action would make foreign buyers stop dealing with Brazil (Unesp).

figures.label: Vale buyout of Caemi, 2001-2006 (total)
figures.note: 16.82% in 2001 for US$278.7 mn; Mitsui stake 2003 for US$426.4 mn; remaining 39.8% in Mar 2006 by share swap, US$2.5 bn.

figures.label: Vale takes 100% of MBR, 2007
figures.value: 231 million for 6.25% of EBM, plus a 30-year lease of 13.75% (US$60.5 mn down plus US$48.1 mn a year)

figures.label: Hanna share of MBR's operating entity (US Bureau of Mines, 1968)
figures.note: Page text did not render. A search snippet says one entity holds 50%, Hanna 34%, State of Minas Gerais the rest; the entity is not named and may be the Caemi holding, not MBR. Do not quote as '34% of MBR'.

summary: In 1962 the Goulart-era government voided Hanna's iron-ore registrations in Minas Gerais. After 1964 the dictatorship changed the rules to let foreign capital in, and Hanna and Caemi formed MBR in 1965. The sources show the new legal framework and the merger, but not the price or how the 1962 order was undone.

title: Fazenda Suiá-Missu and the Xavante of Marãiwatsédé, Mato Grosso
what: The Suiá-Missu estate, founded by Ariosto da Riva. The Xavante were removed in 1966. Estate area is disputed (see figures).
who_got: The Ometto family bought the area in 1962. In the 1970s most went to Liquigás (Italian Ursini group), renamed Liquifarm Agropecuária Suiá-Missú. After Ursini failed in 1978, Agip do Brasil (state-owned ENI/Agip Petroli) absorbed Liquigás and Liquifarm in 1979-81. Price paid by Liquigás: not found. Part (250,000 ha) went to the Brazilian Garavelo group in 1989.
terms: Price not found. Sudam incentives of Cr$7,878,000 went to the Ometto-owned company.
mechanism: Sudam tax incentives are cited by academic sources (the Pública article does not mention them). The Campo-Território text describes fraud in the 1960 registration; no court finding is cited. The Xavante were flown out by FAB aircraft in 1966.
who_paid: The Xavante: about 300 flown out in 1966; a flu and measles epidemic then killed about 80 (about 30% of the group). The Treasury paid the incentives.
after: In 1992 Funai delimited a 200,000 ha Marãiwatsédé land (168,000 ha inside the farm). At Rio-92 Agip/ENI announced the return of about 165,000 ha; this did not happen because the Brazilian subsidiary's shareholders disagreed. Posseiros then invaded. Homologated 1998; Xavante possession only from 2015; about 80% later deforested.
counter_view: The sources say the 1970s sale chain was private-to-private; the public transfer was the incentive and the title (Campo-Território).

figures.label: Estate area
figures.value: 500,000 to about 800,000 ha (695,843 ha in the Sudam table)
figures.note: Sudam 500,000; Ianni 1979 670,000; Sudam table 695,843; about 800,000 after Ariosto da Riva joined the Ometto group; Pública 800,000. Search results also gave 560,000 and 1.7 million (unverified).

figures.value: about 300 flown out in 1966; about 80 died (about 30%)

figures.label: Land Agip announced it would return at Eco-92
figures.note: One search result says 250,000 ha; unresolved.

figures.note: Described as the most deforested Indigenous land in Brazil.

summary: A huge estate in Mato Grosso, helped by Sudam incentives, was sold on to an Italian group and later to Agip. The Xavante were flown out in 1966 and about 80 died in an epidemic. The land was returned in law in 1998 but in practice only from 2015.

title: SUDAM fiscal incentives (Operação Amazônia)
what: The state waived income tax for firms investing in the Amazon, with up to 100% exemption for varying periods on income or import tax. Firms could invest as shareholders in third-party projects (Art. 17) or via branches (Art. 18).
who_got: Mostly agribusiness and cattle ventures, many from the South and Southeast (VW, Ometto group, banks).
terms: By end-1985 SUDAM had approved incentives for 959 firms. Land book value equalled 92% of the projects' own resources, and many firms did not meet job targets.
mechanism: Tax-credit funds under Decreto-Lei 756/1969 (revoked 2001; the Planalto page was not opened, so this is unconfirmed).
who_paid: The Treasury (waived tax), the forest, peasants and posseiros (possession turned into private property in Conceição do Araguaia), and workers.
after: Per the paper, approvals fell by the 1990s and ended in fraud scandals; SUDAM closed in 2001 (not verified).
counter_view: No defence of the incentives (regional development, security goals) was found in the opened sources.

figures.value: US$ 3.928 milhões as printed (likely US$3.9 billion); 959 firms
figures.note: Confirmed only as printed in the Rielo paper. The unit is not explained; Costa 2012 itself was not opened.

figures.label: Land book value as share of projects' own resources
figures.note: Jobs were also under 1% of the peasant-sector workforce in 1985.

figures.label: Large projects in the Conceição do Araguaia region
figures.note: Corrected scope: the original note said 'installed by the regime'. The paper says these are in the Conceição do Araguaia region, not all of the Amazon.

summary: SUDAM waived tax for firms investing in the Amazon, mainly ranches and agribusiness. By 1985 it had approved incentives for 959 firms. No total hectare figure for the Amazon was found.

title: Zona Franca de Manaus (DL 288/1967)
what: Tax exemptions (IPI, import and other taxes) for industry in the Manaus Industrial Pole. DL 288 of 28 Feb 1967 reformulated the 1957 free zone; Suframa was created by Decreto 61.244/1967.
who_got: Assembly plants of mostly foreign and national electronics and motorcycle brands (not detailed in the sources).
terms: Tax exemptions. No figures from 1967-85 were found.
mechanism: Decreto-Lei 288/1967 and tax exemptions for the Manaus pole.
who_paid: The Treasury, as revenue not collected.
after: The regime has been extended and still exists.
counter_view: The Treasury says the fiscal cost has been falling, and defenders call it a constitutional alternative regime, not a waiver (Treasury paper, not opened). The Senate study itself frames the figure as 'renúncia'.

figures.label: Total tax cost, 2011 (ZFM benefits R$17.8 bn plus R$1.4 bn and R$3.2 bn other parts)

figures.label: Treasury view that fiscal cost is falling
figures.note: Treasury paper not opened.

summary: The 1967 decree gave tax exemptions to industry in Manaus. The only cost figure found is modern (R$22.4 bn in 2011). Nothing from 1967-85 was found.

title: Jari Project (Daniel K. Ludwig), Pará and Amapá
what: An enormous private landholding in the Jari valley, plus state-backed finance, and in the end the debt. Size sources disagree (see figures).
who_got: Ludwig bought the firm Empresa de Comércio e Navegação Jari Ltda in 1967. Brazilian law did not limit project area as long as Brazilians own it. In 1981-82 a consortium of 23 Brazilian groups took over; the government pushed businessmen to join as a 'patriotic duty'.
terms: English Wikipedia: 1.6 million acres (6,475 km2) for US$3 mn (the price is unsourced there). Ludwig invested US$845 mn by 1982.
mechanism: Ludwig bought privately. For the exit, per Em Tempo (opposition weekly, partisan): he refused a US$20 mn instalment on a US$200 mn foreign debt guaranteed by the BNDE; the government assumed US$180 mn in exchange for shares without voting rights; BNDE lent Antunes US$35 mn to buy Ludwig's MBR and St John del Rey shares and was released from the guarantee.
who_paid: Per Em Tempo, the treasury and BNDE guarantee. English Wikipedia and CSMonitor say Ludwig got no money and lost US$845 mn, and that the debt passed to the new owners. Caboclo and extractivist communities are also named in the notes (not sourced).
after: The group later passed through other owners. The 2000 sale to Sergio Amoroso's group was for R$1 with about US$400 mn of debt.
counter_view: English Wikipedia and CSMonitor say Ludwig received nothing and lost US$845 mn. Em Tempo says he walked away 'without spending a penny' and kept a rice farm (about US$100 mn), a bauxite deposit (about US$600 mn) and securities (about US$480 mn). Resolving this needs BNDES records, not found.

title: Trombetas bauxite (Mineração Rio do Norte, MRN)
what: Bauxite mining rights and a railway concession in Oriximiná and Porto Trombetas. Decreto 81.889 (5 Jul 1978) gave the right to build and operate the Trombetas railway.
who_got: Vale and Alcan formed MRN (dates differ: 1967 or 1979 in the same source); CBA took 10% in 1973. Later MRN bought the Cruz Alta deposits from Alcoa and Billiton Metais.

mechanism: Mining rights and the railway concession decree.
who_paid: Not found. Impacts on quilombola communities and tax terms were not found.
after: Present owners are Glencore 45%, South32 33% and Rio Tinto 22%. MRN bauxite fed Alumar and the Barcarena smelters.

title: Estatização of external debt (Res. 63 to the 1983-84 project deposits)
what: External debt concentrated in the public sector. Part of the debt first contracted by private firms was moved to the Central Bank, mainly through foreign-currency deposit schemes.
who_got: Private borrowers (industrial groups and banks) whose dollar obligations moved to the Central Bank. Total US$ of private debt absorbed in 1979-85: not found in any opened source.
terms: Not a price. Res. 63 loans grew from about 7% of external debt (1968) to about 20% (1974) and 18.4% of the stock in 1980.
mechanism: Two different instruments. Resolução 63 (21 Aug 1967) let banks and BNDE borrow abroad and on-lend; it is not a transfer to the state. Circular 230 (1974) and Resolução 432 (23 Jun 1977) allowed registered foreign-currency deposits, moving exchange and interest risk to the Central Bank. In 1983-84 'project deposits' made the Central Bank borrower and guarantor of global debt, private and public.
who_paid: The Central Bank balance sheet, then the Treasury, financed by monetary expansion and domestic debt (IPEA); in the CPI da Dívida reading, taxpayers via the Brady transfer.
after: The 1990s Brady operation (about US$50 bn) transferred US$28 bn of Central Bank liabilities to the Treasury.
counter_view: Meira and Cruz present the rise of public debt mainly as a result of state firms' borrowing for the II PND and of the creditors' cartel and IMF conditions after 1982, not only a rescue of private debtors. Carneiro (2002) calls state firms' borrowing the 'traditional' channel. The Auditoria Cidadã chapter is advocacy and says 'estatização' does not appear in its own text.

title: Federal-highway land strips (DL 1.164/1971) and Transamazônica colonisation

who_got: The note's link to ranches and companies is an inference (cases on SUDAM, VW and Suiá-Missu). No source gives the volume of strip land sold.
terms: Not applicable. Art. 3 had INCRA recognise legitimate possession; Indigenous rights were reserved.
mechanism: Decreto-Lei 1.164 of 1 Apr 1971 (terras devolutas in the Legal Amazon). Revoked by DL 2.375 of 24 Nov 1987, which removed the 'indispensable' status except in the border strip. 'Returned to the states' is not verified.
who_paid: Indigenous peoples: a 2013 report says the road affected 29 groups, 11 of them isolated. Settlers: the plan was for about 100,000 families but no more than 8,000 were settled in the three Pará poles (Marabá, Altamira, Itaituba).
after: Integrated Colonisation Programs closed in late 1978 after land-title conflicts.

title: Itaipu: contracts and beneficiaries
what: The binational dam. Fit with 'public to private' is weak: the sources document cost and debt, not contractor margins.
who_got: Civil works went to the Brazilian consortium Unicon (five firms) and the Paraguayan Conempa (six), 1975 contract. Unicon members per Itaipu's transparency page (Cetenco, CBPO, Camargo Corrêa, Andrade Gutierrez, Mendes Júnior) are unverified. Financed by Eletrobras (main creditor), BNDES, Banco do Brasil, and originally about 70 financiers with Treasury guarantees.
terms: Contract prices not found.
mechanism: Tariff 'pelo passivo': the tariff covers operating costs and debt service, so debt costs go directly to consumers.
who_paid: Brazilian and Paraguayan consumers through the tariff. Utilities' arrears were about US$4 bn in the early 1990s, with a Paraguayan dispute over about US$4 bn of the debt.
after: Debt paid off in Feb 2023. The 2009 deal raised Paraguay's compensation by 200% (Brazil's payments from about US$120 mn to US$360 mn a year by 2011).
counter_view: Itaipu is a working, amortised asset (record 98,630 GWh in 2013, CPDOC). The controversy is the debt's dollar charge and the contractors' margins, which could not be documented.

figures.value: budget US$10.3 bn; about US$16.2 bn estimated in 1991; about US$12.5 bn nominal per Itaipu

title: Tucuruí dam and subsidised power for Albras, Alunorte and Alumar
what: Subsidised electricity from a state dam for Japanese-owned (Albras and Alunorte with CVRD) and Alcoa/Billiton-owned (Alumar) aluminium smelters. More than half of Tucuruí's energy goes to electro-intensive mineral industry; 64.3% of Pará's 2003 generation fed them.
who_got: Albras and Alunorte (NAAC: 32 private firms 60% plus the Japanese government 40%; CVRD 51% in the original project; agreements 20 Jun 1978) and Alumar. Contractor Camargo Corrêa. Vale sold its Albras stake to Hydro (2011).
terms: Original price: a 1976 protocol set a price tied to aluminium with a minimum of 8 mills/kWh; the tariff approved in Aug 1979 was 10.5 mills/kWh (blog source, no primary document). By 2004 Albras paid about R$34 (US$11-12) per MWh and Alumar almost double. After 2004 Albras won an auction at the R$53/MWh ceiling; Alumar about R$60/MWh.
mechanism: A 1976 protocol and a 1979 tariff, with the state taking over the cost of the hydro plant (Pinto: 'o governo federal decidiu assumir completamente o custo da usina', meaning Tucuruí, not the smelter). The state energy monopoly was bent to let the Japanese hold up to a third of Eletronorte shares; they never joined the works.
who_paid: Treasury and Eletronorte, electricity consumers (the difference falls on non-favoured consumers, mainly households), and riverside populations: 1,100 islands formed with 6,500 people on them, and compensation is still litigated.
after: Contract renewed 1 May 2004 for 20 years (US$3.4 bn, US$170 mn a year), with profit-sharing when aluminium exceeds US$1,450/t. Eletronorte wanted US$20-22/MWh and Albras offered about US$15.
counter_view: The design tied price to the aluminium price with a floor and later a profit-share clause, and the contracts anchored demand for a dam Eletronorte could not otherwise sell. Eletrobras filings describe the 2004 price as a floor at Tucuruí's break-even tariff plus an aluminium premium (SEC filing, page not opened, unverified). The government and Eletronorte argument that cheap power was the condition for export earnings was not found in an opened source.

title: Fazenda Vale do Rio Cristalino (Volkswagen), Santana do Araguaia, Pará
what: A ranch of about 139,000 ha run by VW's subsidiary Companhia Vale do Rio Cristalino, acquired in 1974, with SUDAM tax incentives and low-interest loans.
who_got: Volkswagen, through its subsidiary. Repórter Brasil and prosecutors say it was acquired 'in a consortium with the military government'; Pública does not say 'consortium' and says it was financed by SUDAM and Banco da Amazônia (Basa). Sold in 1986 to the Matsubara group, which inherited the debts.
terms: No original SUDAM amount found.
mechanism: SUDAM incentives and low-interest loans.
who_paid: Workers (forced-labour allegations 1974-86), the Treasury and the forest. About 300 officially employed; clearing was done by informal workers recruited by 'gatos', some under 18. The investigation rests on at least 42 victims and 11 witnesses.
after: The labour prosecutor (MPT) filed a civil action in Dec 2024 seeking R$165 mn. The Redenção labour court ordered R$165 mn in collective moral damages, upheld by TRT-8. Four former workers won R$2 mn each in individual suits (12 Jun 2026). The judge rejected the time-bar argument and held VW responsible as the main shareholder. The two outcomes are separate, not conflicting.
counter_view: Volkswagen denies responsibility for the Pará ranch, does not comment on ongoing proceedings, and has appealed (Repórter Brasil).

figures.label: Public funds received (prosecutors)
figures.note: Not found in either cited page. Repórter Brasil gives only the collective claim of US$29.2 mn. Needs the MPT complaint.

title: 1975 Brazil-Germany nuclear deal and Nuclebrás
government: Geisel (project run by Paulo Nogueira Batista at Nuclebrás)
what: Two 1,300 MW reactors by 1985 with an option for six more by 1990; enrichment (jet nozzle), fuel fabrication and pilot reprocessing; up to 20% of Brazilian uranium ore to Germany. Nuclebrás was created Dec 1974; agreement signed in Bonn 27 Jun 1975. Fit with 'public to private' is weak.
who_got: Kraftwerk Union/Siemens (reactors), German banks (loans) and Nuclep (heavy equipment, created 1975 with Germans). Contract-level terms and prices are unverified.
terms: Value is a range of US$4-10 bn (see figures).
mechanism: An intergovernmental agreement and state company Nuclebrás.
who_paid: The Treasury and Eletrobras/Nuclebrás (state financing). Costs 'ballooned with little demonstrable result' (Wilson Center). Nuclebrás' total debt: not found.
after: Scaled back from 1978. Angra 2 (planned 1985) operated only in 2000/2001. Angra 3, under construction since 1986, has consumed more than R$20 bn (DW/Forte, 2025). Of eight planned plants, one runs and one is unfinished. The jet-nozzle company was liquidated in 1993. A parliamentary inquiry (CPI) about 1978 is cited but was not opened (unverified).
counter_view: The aim was energy security after the 1973 oil shock and the US cancelling enriched uranium for Angra 1. It became a parallel autonomous Navy enrichment programme from 1979 (Atlas FGV). Jet-nozzle enrichment was unproven (Wilson Center).

figures.label: Value of the deal
figures.value: about US$10 bn at 1975 prices (Atlas FGV); up to DM10 bn, about US$4 bn (Gray 2012 via pt.wikipedia)
figures.note: The larger figure is a German export projection (DW via https://www.forte.jor.br/2025/04/14/o-fracasso-do-acordo-nuclear-entre-o-brasil-e-a-alemanha/). Gray 2012: https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programa_nuclear_brasileiro

figures.label: Brazil payment and German loan
figures.value: DM2.25 bn paid by Brazil; German loan of DM4.3 bn
figures.note: Seen in a snippet only.

summary: Brazil signed a 1975 nuclear deal with West Germany worth US$4-10 bn on the sources' estimates. Costs ballooned and the programme was scaled back from 1978. Contract prices and Nuclebrás debt were not found.

title: Proálcool: subsidies to sugar mills and distilleries
what: Subsidised credit to mills and distillery builders, price parity with sugar for ethanol, an obligation on Petrobras to buy all alcohol, and levies on gasoline, diesel and lubricants to cover costs.
who_got: Mill and distillery owners (Ferro: 'usineiros inadimplentes' sustained by the public purse). Named beneficiaries and loan-level data: not found.
terms: Credit with negative real interest, 3 years' grace and 12 years to repay (from a search snippet of a paper, unverified).
mechanism: Subsidised credit, price parity, mandatory Petrobras purchase and fuel levies.
who_paid: Petrobras (Conta Álcool), Banco do Brasil and the financial system, and gasoline consumers through the levies (per Ferro and biodieselbr).
after: 1989-90 supply crisis; a 'MEG' blend of 60% ethanol, 34% methanol and 6% gasoline; imports of ethanol and methanol above 1 bn litres in 1989-95. The sector is clear but the money total is not; a proper fiscal study is needed.
counter_view: Foreign-exchange savings of about US$11.5 bn in 1975-2000 and output peaking at 12.3 bn litres in 1986-87 (biodieselbr, trade site). An FGV article reportedly says official savings claims of US$9 bn were cut to under US$3 bn by a later study (scan not readable, unverified).

title: Programa Grande Carajás: tax regime and pig-iron smelters

who_got: Firms processing the ore; dozens of charcoal pig-iron smelters later clustered along the Carajás railway (Açailândia, MA). The ore itself was held by CVRD (state): US Steel left the AMZA joint venture in 1977 with a US$50 mn indemnity. IPI and import-duty exemptions were not confirmed.

mechanism: Decreto-Lei 1.813 (24 Nov 1980); DL 1.825 (22 Dec 1980); extension to 31 Dec 1990 by DL 2.152/1984; Decreto 85.387/1980 created the approving interministerial council; Decreto 86.417/1981 (not opened) extended it to Albras-Alunorte.
who_paid: Concentration of income and large estates; a mineral enclave for export; forest loss to charcoal.
after: Time-limited exemptions were later extended (to 1990).

what: A programme to pave about 1,500 km of BR-364 and resettle migrants, financed with the World Bank. Mostly a state project; the private-interest angle (land speculation, ranchers following the road) is not documented in the sources. Weak fit.
who_got: Not applicable (public programme).
terms: Not applicable.
mechanism: A World Bank-financed public programme.
who_paid: Indigenous peoples and the forest. About 150,000 migrants came to Rondônia in 1984 against INCRA lots for 5,000 families (unverified). Of 55 Indigenous areas only 4 were fully protected; Rondônia had the fastest deforestation in the Amazon.
after: The Bank suspended payments in Feb 1985, its first halt over environment and Indigenous rights. After the halt the government demarcated about 1.8 million ha.

who_got: Agropecuária Capemi and firms linked to one person (alleged).
terms: Financed with a US$100 mn loan from Banco Nacional de Paris, US$25 mn guaranteed by BNCC, about US$27 mn of external resources in total.
mechanism: A pension-fund company contracted for timber clearing; state-backed guarantee.
who_paid: The pension fund members and the state-backed guarantor. An intervention and a 1980s CPI followed (per the same page).
after: Contract cancelled in March 1983. Weak sourcing; do not conflate with the Delfin case.

title: Coroa-Brastel (1983)
government: Figueiredo; ministers Delfim Netto (Planning) and Ernane Galvêas (Finance); Central Bank president Carlos Langoni
what: Liquidity support and a Caixa Econômica Federal loan (1981) to Assis Paim Cunha's Coroa/Brastel group. The loan amount was not found. The Central Bank made 'several large liquidity injections'; Paim asked for a Cr$30 bn credit line, which forced an inspection.
who_got: Paim's financial and brokerage group (Coroa, Brastel, and the Laureano brokerage, linked by DCM to a Golbery family connection; not a finding).
terms: Not found.
mechanism: Central Bank assistance lines and a Caixa loan; regulators suspended inspections. On 30 May 1983 Delfim told Langoni that Paim had liquidity problems; the Bank intervened in June 1983 and liquidated the group.
who_paid: Letter holders lost most, since Coroa letters had no public guarantee. Later the Treasury: in March 2014 the STF's 1st panel (3-0) held the Central Bank's rescission action time-barred, leaving a judgement for brokerage PEBB of about R$400 mn to be paid by the Treasury.
after: Paim confessed to the fake issues and got 8 years 3 months, appealing free. Delfim and Galvêas were accused of diverting funds via the Caixa loan and acquitted by the STF (pt.wikipedia says charges were filed in 1985).
counter_view: The DCM author says it cannot be proved that Delfim directly favoured Paim, and found no wrongdoing by Langoni.

figures.note: Author's estimate. Another estimate: R$250 mn (updated) and 34,000 people (snippet, unverified).

summary: The Central Bank and the Caixa propped up the Coroa-Brastel group before its 1983 collapse. Letter holders lost most, and the Treasury later owed a judgement of about R$400 mn. Ministers were acquitted. The Caixa loan amount was not found.

title: Delfin (BNH) debt swap, 1982-83
government: Figueiredo; Minister Mario Andreazza (Interior, in charge of BNH)
what: Delfin (Ronald Levinsohn) owed the Banco Nacional da Habitação about Cr$70 bn (about US$250 mn), or Cr$77 bn at intervention. It offered two plots (Barra da Tijuca in Rio and Cotia in São Paulo) at Cr$60.8 bn.
who_got: The Delfin group, which had about 3.5 million savings depositors. Approved with the backing of Andreazza, with Delfim Netto and Galvêas also involved (a claim of the DCM source).
terms: BNH technicians valued the plots at about Cr$6.3 bn, roughly one-sixth of the price accepted; a BNH director resigned. Another account has the land at Cr$9.6 bn (unverified).
mechanism: BNH settled a debt in kind. The swap came out in Folha de S.Paulo on 30 Dec 1982; depositors ran on 3 Jan 1983; the Central Bank intervened and moved accounts to Caixa. O Globo said 'irregular operations diverted Cr$6 bn' of depositors' funds.
who_paid: BNH (a body fed by FGTS) bore the difference between debt and land value. The sources do not say how losses were finally allocated.
after: In 1991 Levinsohn agreed to pay the rest in 13 years and, per DCM, no instalment was paid. In March 2006 the STJ accepted payment with the two plots on a 'potential value' basis (some sources say STF, unverified).
counter_view: The defence's potential-value valuation, which the STJ accepted, treats the land as worth more once built on.

title: Sulbrasileiro, Comind, Auxiliar and Maisonnave bank failures (1985)
what: The Central Bank intervened in Sulbrasileiro on 7 Feb 1985. In May 1985 the federal government created Banco Meridional do Brasil and expropriated Sulbrasileiro's shares by decree-law. On 19 Nov 1985 Maisonnave, Comind and Auxiliar were liquidated the same day by decree-law.
who_got: Banco Meridional received about 15,000 items: 5,000 beach plots on ten beaches and 80,000-90,000 ha of rural property. The Maisonnave group got US$20 mn from the Central Bank in a rediscount line.
terms: Not applicable.
mechanism: Decree-law expropriation of shares (the decree-law number 7315/1985 printed in English Wikipedia looks odd, unverified). Liquidation by decree-law is presented as the only time Sarney used one to revoke bank charters.
who_paid: For Sulbrasileiro, taxpayers through a federally created successor (one headline says shareholders would not be compensated; unclear). For the three Nov 1985 banks, creditors and clients; the sources give no Treasury cost.
after: A Maisonnave debt of R$406 mn was still on the books in a CMN record of 27 Nov 1997. No verified total public cost for 1983-85 bank rescues was found.
counter_view: The Meridional solution was pushed by Rio Grande do Sul politicians, a political rescue of a regional bank rather than of owners. Comind, Auxiliar and Maisonnave were liquidated rather than rescued, so this is less a transfer than a failed rescue.

title: Calha Norte (1985)
